A PhD studentship is available with Dr. Mitch Weegman in the Department of Biology at the University of Saskatchewan (https://www.ducks.ca/our-work/science/saskatchewan-endowed-chair/), co-supervised by Dr. Jolene Giacinti (Environment and Climate Change Canada), in collaboration with Dr. John Coluccy (Ducks Unlimited Inc.).
 Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) continues to cause outbreaks in wild birds and domestic poultry in Canada, with significant implications for wildlife conservation, agriculture, and One Health.
 To better understand the waterfowl–poultry interface and associated transmission risks, the student will investigate how GPS-tracked waterfowl use the immediate surroundings of commercial poultry and dairy farms and how these local interactions may relate to HPAI risk. This is an analysis-focused project using existing datasets; no new field data collection is planned. The work involves sensitive datasets and strict adherence to confidentiality and data-governance protocols will be required. There will be opportunities for field work on related projects across North America for the student to build field experiences during the graduate program. 
 The student and research team will develop research questions that support a common goal of understanding fine-scale patterns of waterfowl use near farms and implications for HPAI transmission. There is substantial opportunity for the student to lead on development of objectives/manuscripts. Primary objectives for the student will be to:
 1.       Quantify local habitat use by tagged waterfowl in the vicinity of poultry and dairy premises.
2.       Assess overlap between waterfowl movements and farm locations, including farms with and without historical HPAI detections, and evaluate how nearby habitat/farm characteristics relate to this overlap.
3.       Synthesize implications for biosecurity, wildlife conservation, and One Health related to HPAI at the wildlife–agriculture interface.
 Prerequisites: Ideal candidates will have an MSc in ecology, statistics or a closely related field.  Location: Dept. of Fish, Wildlife, & Conservation Biology, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO 
 Description: The Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Conservation Biology at Colorado State University invites applications for a funded PhD student position to study ecology and management of nonnative Mysis shrimp in Grand Lake, Colorado. The successful applicant will be based in the laboratories of Dr. Zoe Almeida and Dr. Dan Preston. Nonnative species can restructure food webs, and Mysis have exemplified such consequences following their introduction from their native Great Lakes region to lakes throughout the Western US. In Grand Lake, where a trans-basin water project has contributed to reduced water clarity, there is strong interest in exploring whether reducing Mysis may restore native zooplankton populations and improve water clarity. The successful candidate will design and conduct research to assess how Mysis affect water clarity through food web interactions in experimental settings, especially using laboratory mesocosms. Research may also include leveraging long-term data on water quality and fish populations, in-lake mesocosm experiments, gut content and stable isotope analyses, bioenergetic modeling, and evaluating the ecological roles of Mysis at broader spatial scales using data synthesis. The successful candidate will collaborate with partners and stakeholders at CSU, Colorado Parks and Wildlife, Northern Water, the Three Lakes Watershed Association, and the Bureau of Reclamation. 
 Candidates must have: 
-       An undergraduate degree in limnology, ecology, biology, or equivalent 
-       Demonstrated excellence in science communication (scientific writing, presentations) and quantitative skills 
-       Ability to communicate clearly and work collaboratively with a research team 
 Preferred qualifications include:             
-       A Masters degree in a related field and demonstrated ability to publish research 
-       Experience with experimental design, limnology, fish ecology, and food web analyses (e.g., gut content, stable isotope, and metabarcoding analyses) 
-       Experience working with multiple stakeholders 
-       Familiarity with common programs used for data analyses (e.g., R software) 
 Position Start Date: Preferred start date is summer of 2026, which would provide the opportunity for field work before enrolling as a graduate student in Fall of 2026. A later start date is negotiable, but the ideal candidate would formally enroll during the '26/'27 academic year. 
 Funding: The position is conditionally funded for 4 years through support from the Bureau of Reclamation and teaching assistantships. Funding includes stipend, health insurance, and tuition.

 Location: Dept. of Fish, Wildlife, & Conservation Biology, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO 
 Description: The Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Conservation Biology at Colorado State University invites applications for a funded PhD student position to study ecology and management of nonnative Mysis shrimp in Grand Lake, Colorado. The successful applicant will be based in the laboratories of Dr. Zoe Almeida and Dr. Dan Preston. Nonnative species can restructure food webs, and Mysis have exemplified such consequences following their introduction from their native Great Lakes region to lakes throughout the Western US. In Grand Lake, where a trans-basin water project has contributed to reduced water clarity, there is strong interest in exploring whether reducing Mysis may restore native zooplankton populations and improve water clarity. The successful candidate will design and conduct research to assess how Mysis affect water clarity through food web interactions in experimental settings, especially using laboratory mesocosms. Research may also include leveraging long-term data on water quality and fish populations, in-lake mesocosm experiments, gut content and stable isotope analyses, bioenergetic modeling, and evaluating the ecological roles of Mysis at broader spatial scales using data synthesis. The successful candidate will collaborate with partners and stakeholders at CSU, Colorado Parks and Wildlife, Northern Water, the Three Lakes Watershed Association, and the Bureau of Reclamation. 
 Candidates must have: 
-       An undergraduate degree in limnology, ecology, biology, or equivalent 
-       Demonstrated excellence in science communication (scientific writing, presentations) and quantitative skills 
-       Ability to communicate clearly and work collaboratively with a research team 
 Preferred qualifications include:             
-       A Masters degree in a related field and demonstrated ability to publish research 
-       Experience with experimental design, limnology, fish ecology, and food web analyses (e.g., gut content, stable isotope, and metabarcoding analyses) 
-       Experience working with multiple stakeholders 
-       Familiarity with common programs used for data analyses (e.g., R software) 
 Position Start Date: Preferred start date is summer of 2026, which would provide the opportunity for field work before enrolling as a graduate student in Fall of 2026. A later start date is negotiable, but the ideal candidate would formally enroll during the '26/'27 academic year. 
 Funding: The position is conditionally funded for 4 years through support from the Bureau of Reclamation and teaching assistantships. Funding includes stipend, health insurance, and tuition. 
 Application: Please submit a letter of interest (1 page), a CV, and contact information for three references as one PDF file to: Dr. Zoe Almeida (l.zoe.almeida@colostate.edu) and Dr. Dan Preston (Dan.Preston@colostate.edu) (please use subject “PhD application: Mysis experiments”). Finalists will be invited to apply through the Colorado State University Graduate School. 
 Closing Date: Review begins immediately with interviews on a rolling basis and will continue until the position is filled.

The Bowes Lab at Emporia State University is seeking a highly motivated student for a fully funded M.S. thesis position focused on sea turtle ecology, movement, and foraging dynamics using stable isotope analysis.

This project is part of an ongoing collaborative research program integrating stable isotopes, genetics, and field-based conservation to better understand sea turtle habitat use and population connectivity in the Gulf of Mexico.

Position Details

Start Date: Summer/Fall 2026 (flexible) 
Duration: 2 years 
Funding Package: 
$15,600+ annual stipend 
Full tuition and fees covered 
Research Overview

The student will contribute to a multidisciplinary collaborative project examining:

Sea turtle foraging ecology and movement patterns 
Stable isotope analysis of carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen 
Integration with genetic lineage data (e.g., natal origin) 
Applications to conservation and management under changing environmental conditions 
Field and collaborative opportunities may include work with partners such as Sea Turtle Inc. and other conservation agencies.

Qualifications

Preferred candidates will have:

B.S. or B.A. in Biology, Ecology, Marine Science, or a related field 
Strong interest in aquatic ecology, conservation, or marine systems 
Experience with (or willingness to learn): 
Stable isotope techniques 
Field sampling and lab processing 
Data analysis in R or similar platforms 
Strong work ethic, independence, and collaborative mindset 

How to Apply

Interested applicants should email the following materials:

Curriculum Vitae (CV) 
Brief Statement of Interest (1 page or less) 
Send materials to: rebowes.ecology@gmail.com

Review of applications will begin immediately and continue until May 1.

The Bowes Lab is based within the School of Science and Mathematics and the Prophet Aquatic Research and Outreach Center (PAROC) at Emporia State University (https://www.emporia.edu/) and focuses on aquatic food webs, stable isotope ecology, and applied conservation research across freshwater and marine systems. https://rebowesecology.com/

Description
The Berigan lab (https://liamaberigan.github.io) at Auburn University College of Forestry, Wildlife and Environment is hiring a PhD student to research quantitative methods for modeling animal movement. The successful applicant will apply Bayesian state-space models or related techniques to large datasets, including both GPS and Motus data, to build improved movement models for avian migration. We anticipate this position to be highly collaborative and will focus mostly on leveraging preexisting datasets. While certain aspects of the project are well defined, there is considerable opportunity for the student to develop chapters that suite their own interests, especially in the realm of movement ecology. Fieldwork will be up to the discretion of the student, with example projects including Motus tag deployments on birds (e.g., Henslow’s Sparrows, American Woodcock) or drones.

Minimum qualifications:

·      Master’s degree (awarded or anticipated) in biology, statistics, or a related discipline
·      Extensive experience working with the programming language R
·      Strong communication skills in oral and written English
·      Ability to work independently and as part of an interdisciplinary team
·      Self-motivation, a positive attitude, and strong interpersonal skills

Desired qualifications:

·      Interest in statistics and quantitative methods, especially Bayesian hierarchical modeling
·      Experience collecting and/or analyzing avian movement data, especially using the Motus network
·      If fieldwork is of interest, experience handling and tagging birds
·      Record of publication in peer-reviewed journals

The successful applicant will be asked to apply to Auburn University’s College of Forestry, Wildlife and Environment for admission in Fall 2026, and will be expected to arrive prior to the first day of classes (August 17th). Note that GRE scores are not required for admission but may create opportunities for additional funding support (e.g., Auburn Presidential Graduate Opportunity Program). If you have GRE scores, please submit them as a part of your application package.

Compensation: Stipend of $30,000 per year, plus a tuition waiver. 

How to apply: Please email Dr. Liam Berigan (lib0016@auburn.edu) a single PDF document containing a 1) cover letter, 2) CV, 3) unofficial transcripts from all colleges attended, 4) GRE scores (if available), and 5) contact information for 3 professional references. Please title your email “PhD application” to ensure it is routed correctly. Application deadline is April 21st, but I encourage you to apply early as applications will be evaluated on a rolling basis until a suitable candidate is found. More information about our graduate program can be found here: https://cfwe.auburn.edu/graduate-study/graduate-degrees/.

Contact
Dr. Liam Berigan
lib0016@auburn.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
PhD Assistantship - Silviculture after the Storm: Tornado Recovery Strategies for Mature Oak Forests

The Forest Dynamics and Management Lab at the University of Kentucky invites qualified applications for a funded PhD assistantship under the guidance of Dr. Lance A. Vickers. The student will work closely with collaborators from the USDA Forest Service Northern Research Station and the Hoosier National Forest to explore forest management strategies to wind disturbances. This project offers a unique field experiment evaluating how many silvicultural decisions - including salvage logging, planting strategies, & timber stand improvement - drive forest recovery in mature oak forests following a tornado. 

The selected candidate will engage in cutting-edge research including:
• Assessing how silviculture influences regeneration success, stand composition, long-term productivity, and resilience following a natural disaster.
• Investigating how regeneration strategies (natural, locally-sourced seedlings, assisted migration, and assisted range expansion) shape forest recovery.
• Examining the role of white-tailed deer browsing across different regeneration strategies, planting densities, and configurations. 

Funding and Benefits:
• Competitive stipend, tuition coverage, and benefits options.
• Additional funding for research-related travel and professional development.

Applicants must have: 
• Strong interest in forest ecology, silviculture, and applied management.
• Excellent communication and collaborative teamwork skills.
• Experience and willingness to conduct extensive fieldwork under variable conditions.
• An MS degree in forestry, ecology, or a related field; experience with R and GIS software is a plus.

Applicants should submit: 1) A cover letter outlining research interests and relevant experience; 2) A current CV; 3) Unofficial academic transcripts; and 4) Three professional references to: lance.vickers@uky.edu. Application review will begin immediately and continue until filled; only those selected for interview will be contacted. Anticipated start: Fall 2026 preferred.

Contact
Lance Vickers

Description
A fully funded M.S. (2) or Ph.D. (1) position is available to join a collaborative research project focused on advancing conservation and management of northern bobwhite through cutting-edge remote sensing and quantitative ecology.

Project Overview

This project integrates remote sensing, field ecology, and advanced statistical modeling to better understand how habitat structure and composition influence bobwhite populations across spatial scales.

The selected student will contribute to two primary objectives:

Objective 1: Landscape Mapping Using Remote Sensing

The student will develop spatial datasets to distinguish native grass-dominated systems from exotic grass pastures and quantify shrub cover across study landscapes.

Key approaches include:

Multispectral and hyperspectral satellite imagery

Vegetation indices (e.g., NDVI) and phenological signatures

Machine learning classification methods

LiDAR (USGS 3DEP; Q2) for shrub structure mapping

Integration of NAIP imagery and potential use of GEDI or SAR data

This component will result in high-resolution habitat maps to support ecological analyses and management decisions.

Objective 2: Multi-scale Habitat Selection of Northern Bobwhite

The student will quantify bobwhite habitat selection across micro-site, patch, and landscape scales using radio-telemetry data.

Field and analytical components include:

Intensive telemetry (year-round tracking)

Micro-site vegetation sampling (structure, composition, ground cover)

Patch-scale GIS analysis (composition, connectivity, edge density)

Integration of land management data (fire, grazing, etc.)

A central component of the project will be development of a Structural Equation Model (SEM) to:

Link habitat characteristics across scales

Quantify direct and indirect drivers of habitat selection

Evaluate mechanistic pathways influencing survival and reproduction

Preferred candidates will have:

B.S. or M.S. in wildlife ecology, ecology, natural resources, or related field

Strong interest in upland game bird ecology and conservation

Experience (or willingness to learn) R, GIS, and statistical modeling

Description
University of Tennessee, Knoxville (UTK) Graduate Assistantship – Evaluating success in aquatic connectivity restorations 

We are accepting applications for a M.S. or PhD graduate student research assistant that would develop a thesis or dissertation evaluating aquatic animal movements and the effectiveness of restorations of connectivity in stream ecosystems. 

Duties: In addition to classes and other requirements of the M.S. in Wildlife and Fisheries Science or the PhD in Natural resources program, the student will complete teaching assistant duties, lead their own comprehensive research project, and assist on other research projects. The objectives of the project that the student will address some or all of the following:

(1)    Characterizing changes in stream animal assemblages, habitat, and the spatial distribution of animals in response to connectivity restorations, including dam removals and aquatic organism passage (AOP) measures at dams and road-stream crossings
(2)     Measuring the dispersal capacity of select stream animals
(3)    Investigating the role of physical habitat characteristics, species life history, movement capacity, and the location and magnitude of potential source populations on the likelihood that species will recolonize an area in response to aquatic connectivity restoration

This assistantship will involve extensive and intensive field work, to be conducted in Tennessee and other locations where aquatic connectivity restorations have recently been completed or are ongoing/planned. Field research activities will involve sampling mobile stream organisms (primarily fishes) with multiple gears (i.e., backpack and/or boat electrofishing, seine, snorkeling, various traps etc.), implantation of passive integrated transponder (PIT) tags and marking with visual implant elastomer (VIE), operation of PIT tag arrays and/or portable antennas and may involve extensive travel and overnight stays at/near the field site locations. Lab and office duties will include data and literature reviews, equipment maintenance and construction, statistical analysis, and writing peer-reviewed publications and technical reports. 

Qualifications: Successful master’s degree applicants will have a B.S. degree in Biology, Ecology, Fisheries and Wildlife Science, or a closely related field, and PhD applicants are expected to hold an M.S. in one of the fields listed above. Applicants must meet all other qualifications for admission to the UTK School of Natural Resources Master's or PhD program. Applicants must have a strong desire to work in the field and laboratory and are expected to publish their research findings in peer-reviewed journals and present at professional conferences. Previous experience in aquatic field research, use of PIT tags and VIE marking techniques, data analysis using statistical software, and data management skills are preferred. The student must also possess a valid driver's license. Successful candidates will also have demonstrated the ability to manage multiple competing tasks for their time (e.g., writing, data collection, coursework), excellent abilities to work in a team setting, are goal oriented and self-directed.

Funding and Timeline: Guaranteed financial support is available for 2 years for a Master’s student or 3 years for a PhD student, beginning in August of 2026. Financial support includes a stipend, tuition, and insurance. Review of applications will begin on March 25th, 2026 and new applications will not be accepted after April 7th, 2026.

1) Personal statement of research interests and career goals

2) Resume or curriculum vitae

3) Transcripts (unofficial is OK)

4) Contact information for three references

Contact
Lisa Izzo & Augustin Engman
lizzo1@utk.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
A M.S.-level research project investigating ecosystem impacts of Common Carp and White Sucker recolonization at Lake Ogallala following a chemical renovation in 2023 and potential for targeted removals to sustain fishery benefits. In an open system, immigration or density-dependent compensatory responses may result in stable or increasing nuisance populations. In Lake Ogallala, high densities of Carp and White Sucker contribute to the degradation of the system through uprooting or ingestion of submerged aquatic vegetation resulting in a loss of macrophyte and macroinvertebrate production. Fish exclosures to protect macrophyte production in tandem with targeted fish removals may be able to maintain trophic conditions. Models involving population structure and dynamics of each species may provide insights as to whether biomass may be suppressed for longer benefits to other recreationally important fishes. 

Completion of the project will serve as partial fulfillment of the requirements for a MS degree from the University of Nebraska at Kearney (UNK). Other requirements include satisfactory completion of coursework, successful thesis defense, and submission of manuscripts for publication.  Each student will be supported on a year-round research assistantship, which includes monthly pay, full tuition waiver, and optional student health insurance. 

Qualifications: B.S. in fisheries or wildlife science/management, population ecology, environmental science, or related field. Experience in fisheries field work, understanding of recreational fisheries management, and data analysis is highly desirable, especially in a competitive selection process. Candidates with demonstrated written and oral communication skills, analytical skills, and strong academic credentials are preferred. Applicants must be self-motivated, demonstrate a strong work ethic, and be capable and willing to work long hours (within boundaries) to complete all aspects of the research, including in the field, laboratory, and office.

One M.S. assistantship in toucan ecology and seed dispersal is available in the Department of Natural Resource Ecology and Management at Iowa State University beginning in August 2026. The student will be advised by Dr. Landon Jones and will largely work with available movement data collected on two species of toucans in a fragmented secondary rainforest landscape in Costa Rica to estimate spatial patterns of seed dispersal in an agent-based modeling framework. Job Title: MS Graduate Research Assistantship, University of Wyoming

Location: Laramie, WY 

Overview: Dr. Kelly Dunning & Associate Dean Professor Temple Stoellinger are recruiting a student to join the Wildlife & Wilderness Recreation Lab in the Haub School of Environment and Natural Resources at the University of Wyoming. 

The Wildlife & Wilderness Recreation Lab works on sustainable nature-based tourism, hunting and fishing, and outdoor recreation issues in Wyoming and the Intermountain West. Our research focuses on public policy of wildlife, recreation, and natural resources making our research practical and impactful to resource management. The MS student will work on a project studying voluntary conservation activities for species like elk, deer, and grouse on oil and gas concessions. The MS student will have interdisciplinary opportunities to provide support to the Wildlife & Wilderness Recreation Lab as needed (please see: wildlifewildernessrecreationlab.org). Our lab has experience working with students of diverse backgrounds, veterans, and non-conventional students, and all are welcome to apply. 

Duties: The Graduate Research Assistant will focus on voluntary conservation activities and relevant conservation laws and policies for species protections on oil and gas concessions on both private land and leases of federal and state public land. This position is ideal for people who want to work in conservation with insights that are valuable to the private sector. This pragmatic focus allows you to follow political priorities of the current administration and be competitive on the job market.  

Ideal candidates for this position will possess outstanding written and oral communication skills, an interest in conservation, and a willingness to write research independently. 

Candidates should have experience 1) working as part of a team on conservation social science, wildlife, or environmental politics and policy in the United States or similar topics, 2) conducting research or outreach in natural or social science. Students with prior work experience in sectors like service or retail are encouraged to list these experiences on their resume as well as it demonstrates independence and ability to work with the public. Candidates should have an interest in fish and wildlife in the Intermountain West, oil and gas, wilderness recreation, and/or an appreciation for federal land recreation and tourism. Candidates should show in their cover letter examples of their ability to work independently. Preferred candidates will have experience with 1) wildlife science or social science such as hunter or angler surveys, political science/public policy/economics, 2) statistical analysis, 3) social science methods/surveys/human dimensions/interview methodologies, 4) scientific or academic writing. Students must possess a valid drivers license and be willing and able to conduct field work in rural communities that may require significant time spent outdoors and in nature. 

Start Date: Fall 2026 in Laramie, Wyoming 

End Date: An MS in the Wildlife & Wilderness Recreation Lab requires 5 semesters of field work and courses ending at the conclusion of spring term 2027 (fall ‘26, spring ‘27, summer ‘27, fall ‘27, spring ‘28). Dunning and Stoellinger will provide close supervision and career planning support to ensure completion on time. 

Degree information: The candidate(s) selected will pursue their MS through the University of Wyoming’s Environment, Natural Resources, and Society program (ENRS). A funded MS covers required credits of tuition and fees during the fall/spring/summer semesters and student health insurance. 

Qualifications: Preference will be given to applicants with interest and/or experience in hunting/fishing surveys, outdoor recreation, and/or interdisciplinary research. Applicants should have a bachelor's degree and a strong positive professional reference from a few previous supervisors. Applicants who have a BA or BS in any field will be considered, with preference given to social science, fish and wildlife science, natural resources, political science, business, or interdisciplinary fields. Applicants must have an undergraduate GPA of 3.0 or higher. Standardized test scores (e.g., GRE) are not required although they can be used to supplement weaker applications. Candidates from all backgrounds are encouraged to apply. Veterans and spouse/children dependents are encouraged to apply. Legal right to work in the United States will need to be held by the applicant. Formal application to the UW ENRS program is required subsequent to selection of the successful candidate(s). 

Questions: Questions may be asked about the vacancy to Kelly Dunning via email, but all relevant information needed to apply to the vacancies is included in the above description. Due to the extremely high volume of interest of previous positions in the lab, feedback on individual applications is not possible and individual conversations prior to submission of application materials is not possible. 

Funding Package: The stipend for Fall 2026 through summer 2026 will be $23,000 (summer funding is included); the stipend for Fall 2026 through May 2027 will be $16,938. tuition, and health insurance. Graduation is May 2027.  

Application Deadline: March 13, 2026 at 5 p.m. MST, Apply early as review of applications will be on a rolling basis, and positions like this are often filled long before the closing date. 

How to apply: Please send the following materials as one PDF document to Dr. Kelly Dunning at kelly.dunning@uwyo.edu with the subject “Your Name MS Position”. This packet should include as a single combined PDF:
(1) Cover letter/narrative (roughly 1-2 pages) that explains your relevant skills and experience identifying specific requirements outlined in this position description, why you want to study at the Haub School, career goals, and your ability to work independently.  
(2) Resume or CV including degree(s) earned, GPA, and contact information for at least three references 
(3) an unofficial copy of your transcript
(4) a writing sample close to the focus of this MS this can be of any length and on any topic

Next steps: Finalists will be contacted for an interview and an optional short writing task to assess the applicant’s writing skills
Contact
Kelly Dunning
kelly.dunning@uwyo.edu (preferred contact method)

UMaine PhD Assistantship in Fish Environmental RNA (eRNA)

Institutions:  University of Maine, Orono, in collaboration with Dublin City University, Ireland and Queen’s University Belfast, North Ireland.

Responsibilities: The PhD student will advance research of an aquaculture environmental RNA (eRNA) project funded by the U.S. Department of Agriculture in collaboration with agencies in the Republic of Ireland and North Ireland. The project will investigate the scope and application of cutting-edge eRNA technology for assessing fish health from water samples. Specifically, the research will involve a combination of field, laboratory, and bioinformatic approaches aimed at characterizing eRNA in water from aquaculture settings for the assessment of Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) disease, stress and development.  The student will be responsible for conducting fish environmental stress and pathogen exposure experiments, collecting water and tissue DNA and RNA samples, performing laboratory preparation and analysis of samples, analyzing associated bioinformatic datasets, and summarizing research in project reports, a dissertation, and peer-reviewed journal publications.

We are seeking applicants for an M.S. assistantship focused on mottled duck (Anas fulvigula) ecology and management.  Available survey data suggest western Gulf Coast mottled ducks have experienced a long-term population decline, and the species has been identified as a focal species by the Louisiana Department of Wildlife & Fisheries, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and Gulf Coast Joint Venture. This project will involve deploying GPS/GSM implant transmitters on female mottled ducks across the Chenier and Deltaic Plains of Louisiana to evaluate habitat selection and movement characteristics during the breeding and nonbreeding seasons, quantify how movements and habitat selection contribute to survival and nest success, identify habitat characteristics at nesting sites, and assess season-specific survival and cause-specific mortality. RIO GRANDE CUTTHROAT TROUT PHD ASSISTANTSHIP

Description & project background: 

The Pregler Lab at New Mexico State University in the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Conservation Ecology invites applications for a PhD research assistantship focused on Rio Grande cutthroat trout conservation. The successful applicant will begin in the Fall 2026 semester.

Rio Grande cutthroat trout (RGCT) are the southernmost species of cutthroat trout and have experienced a severe decline in both range and abundance, now occupying only ~12 percent of its historical distribution and requires targeted management interventions to support recovery. Major components of the recovery plan detail the need to secure extant populations and reintroduce individuals within their native range in Colorado and New Mexico. Recent efforts to date include development of a multi-source, genetically diverse broodstock for the Rio Grande basin that is used for reintroduction efforts.

Individuals from this multi-source broodstock were stocked at multiple sites throughout the recently restored Rio Costilla watershed which represents one of the largest native fish restoration projects in the country. While recent research has shown that this composite broodstock is more genetically diverse compared to using single source populations there is a need to evaluate how these fish are performing in the wild. The present project has a number of goals:

          1. Evaluate genetic structure and diversity of reintroduced Rio Costilla RGCT populations
                     a. There is also opportunity to develop questions with demographic monitoring data in this system.
          2. Genetic assessment of Rio Grande, Canadian, and Pecos basins. 
                     a. Results will help inform multi-source broodstock development for Canadian & Pecos basins and identify additional source populations for Rio Grande basin.
                     b. Results will also provide an updated genetic assessment for RGCT.
          3. There are additional opportunities for the student to develop their own questions using genetic and demographic data.

This project is a collaborative effort funded by the New Mexico Department of Wildlife and there may be potential to collaborate with other university researchers and agencies. Benefits include a salary range of ~$28-29k/year, full tuition waiver, and subsidized health insurance. Funding will also be available for conference travel, workshop training for data analyses, and safety training (e.g., wilderness first aid). The hired candidate will begin in Fall 2026 and will be based at NMSU in Las Cruces, NM.

How to apply: If interested, please compile the following: (1) a statement of interest that describes your educational and research background, as well as your research interests and how this position fits in your career goals (2) curriculum vitae or resume, (3) contact information for three professional references, and (4) unofficial transcripts compiled in a single PDF and save as ‘Lastname_RGCT_PhD.pdf’.  Applicants are also asked to upload a writing sample in the application portal. Applications should be submitted through the airtable linked here:  https://airtable.com/app3jNqbQZsYstwx7/pagrpU5GqaI6FnSTg/form 

Applications are due 03/18/26 by 11:59p MT. You can learn more about the Pregler Lab at https://preglerlab.com and any questions about the position can be sent to Dr. Kasey Pregler at kpregler@nmsu.edu.   

Qualifications: 

Required: B.S. in fisheries, biology, or related field and possession of a valid U.S. driver’s license. The successful applicant must also meet the minimum requirements for admission to the NMSU Graduate School (3.0 GPA in last two years of undergrad). Applicants should also have demonstrated excellent written and oral communication skills, and an ability to work independently. 

Preference will be given to applicants with an M.S. degree in fisheries, biology, or related field and have experience working in the backcountry and are willing to lead field work crews in backcountry conditions.

Successful candidates will have proficiency in R, and an interest in genetics and working with large datasets. They should also demonstrate the ability to work as part of a team and have a willingness to lead field work crews in remote backcountry locations. Applicants with experience in fish ecology, statistical & genetic analysis, and hierarchical modeling are encouraged to apply.

~$28-29k /year
Full tuition waiver 
Subsidized health insurance

Kasey Pregler
kpregler@nmsu.edu (preferred contact method)

A graduate assistantship for a master’s student is expected to be funded at Colorado State University (Fort Collins, CO) working with Dr. Brian D. Gerber (https://bgerber123.github.io/) at the Colorado Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit and wildlife researchers at Colorado Parks and Wildlife. The graduate research assistantship will cover university tuition, fees, health coverage, and includes a pre-tax monthly pay of $3000/month. The position is expected to start Fall 2026 and be funded through December 2028.

Study Context: Sex and age class are important demographic parameters used in population modeling, in which the results help guide management decisions and annual harvest quotas of large mammals (e.g., elk, bighorn sheep, pronghorn, mule deer). This work will help develop new methodology and workflows that will aid Colorado Parks and Wildlife’s objective of producing robust empirical demographic data and population estimates for harvested wildlife. 

Focus: The focus of this study will be to collect data on the size distribution of elk sex and age classes (cow, calf, bull) to train and test a predictive approach using AI algorithms (developed by Colorado Parks and Wildlife) to classify animals from high-resolution aerial imagery. Field observations and size measurements (via 3D camera) will be collected to help test the accuracy of AI predictions. An additional avenue of exploration may be data collection and AI classification of sex/age class from camera trap images. The student will be expected to develop a project proposal outlining study objectives in coordination with Colorado Parks and Wildlife and a graduate committee at Colorado State University. The student will focus on technological and software workflows to meet study objectives, however, there will likely be field work opportunities as well (e.g., field observations, drone/aerial surveys). Given the trajectory of the wildlife field, the skills gained in this study will likely be desirable for future employers. 

 Preferred Qualifications: 

-          Ungulate field research experience in the intermountain west

-          Experience deploying camera traps and managing large data sets

ROJECT TITLE: Pinyon Jay response to juniper management, Deschutes County, Oregon.

BACKGROUND: Pinyon Jays (PIJA, Gymnorhinus cyanocephalus) have experienced significant, range-wide declines over the past 50 years, and are currently under Status Review for ESA listing. Deschutes County, Oregon represents the northwestern-most extent of the species range and lies far outside the extant range of pinyon pine species. Extensive treatments of juniper woodlands have been expedited throughout western states for restoration of sagebrush ecosystems, sage grouse habitat, and altered fire regimes. However, we lack clear understanding of how these treatments impact PIJA populations.  

Management priorities for PIJA in Oregon include assessing impacts of juniper treatments on PIJA and determining state-wide distribution. The primary goals of this project are to experimentally study how juniper treatments impact occupancy, habitat use, and nesting of PIJA on BLM lands in Deschutes County, Oregon. We are implementing a before-after-control-impact study and use bioacoustics monitoring, point counts, and nest searching methods. The MS project will focus on at least one component of the project. This work is in partnership with the East Cascades Bird Alliance, US Fish and Wildlife, and Deschutes BLM. We also contribute to the PIJA Western Working Group and the PIJA Conservation Action Strategy (CAS). The MS candidate will be expected to coordinate with and contribute findings to larger range-wide intiatives. 

LOCATION & PROGRAM: This position supports a student in the Masters of Science in Natural Resources at Oregon Tech in Klamath Falls, OR. Our MS program started in 2024 and is in the Natural Sciences Department, which also encompasses the MS of Medical Science program, and BS programs in Environmental Science and Biology-Health Science. Program description and requirements are here https://www.oit.edu/academics/degrees/natural-resources 

SUPPORT: This position includes the opportunity for a Graduate Teaching Assistantship for the Academic Years 2026-2026 and 2027-2028. The GTA will teach labs in the 200-level Principles of Biology series for majors, &/or similar courses within the students expertise. GTAs cover two 3-hour sections per term. Oregon Tech is on a quarter system. Fall, Winter, and Spring terms are 11 weeks. Our academic year runs from mid-September to Mid-June.  The GTA provides a per-term stipend and partial tuition remission during the academic year (Fall through Spring terms). In addition, this research assistantship will provide additional part-time stipend during the spring term, and full-time hourly salary over the summer. Some travel costs from Klamath Falls to Bend, OR will be covered. The graduate student will be expected to use their own vehicle, preferably one that can handle rugged, rocky roads to access field sites. If the student would prefer to forgo the GTA position and cover their own academic costs, that would be an option. 

POSITION REQUIREMENTS: The candidate should have a Bachelors degree in Natural Resources, Wildlife, Ecology, Environmental Science or a closely related program of study and should meet the requirements for acceptance into the Masters of Natural Resources program at Oregon Tech. Ideally, the applicant will have at least 2 years of field experience studying birds, particularly nest searching and point counts. Experience with bioacoustics monitoring (ARUs, BirdNET) will be especially helpful. Additionally, experience doing habitat analyses (Occupancy modeling, RSFs, SDMs) using program R and GIS will be very valuable.  The candidate should have proven ability to work independently in remote areas, and as a member of a team, including supervising undergraduates and working with volunteers. 

 

DATES: Start date is flexible. We are beginning the greater project design and implementation this winter 2026, therefore, the candidate could start as early as March, 2026 as a temporary hire. The academic year begins in mid-September, 2026. 

LOCATION: Oregon Tech is in Klamath Falls, OR, a small rural region of south-central Oregon. The field research about 3 hours north, near Bend and Sisters, Oregon in the east Cascades, sage-steppe biome. This region is famous for its scenic beauty, biodiversity, and outdoor recreation including hiking and trail running, mountain biking, skiing, and water sports.  

APPLICATIONS: Please email a cover letter detailing your experience, interest in the project, and career goals, along with your CV to Jherime.kellermann@oit.edu ASAP.  We will review packages as they are received.

Contact
Jherime Kellermann
5418515156

Transforming Climate Action – Uncertain Seas 
 
A PhD Scholarship is available at the Centre for Fisheries Ecosystems Research, Fisheries & Marine Institute, Memorial University, St. John’s, NL, Canada.

The Davis College of Agriculture, Natural Resources, and Design at West Virginia University, through Dr. Carol Arantes’s lab, is recruiting a Master’s or PhD student to begin in Fall 2026 to study how changes in river conditions affect aquatic ecosystems and biodiversity. 

The student will be part of a collaborative, interdisciplinary project examining how global hydraulic infrastructure and river management over the past century have altered river discharge regimes and aquatic ecosystems, and how uncertainty in reconstructed historical records affects confidence in global assessments of river change. Working within a multi-institutional research team, the student will collaborate closely with a modeling group to develop and apply new models and indicators of river processes that integrate hydrologic alteration, river fragmentation, sediment transport, river temperature, and patterns of fish diversity and abundance. 

The student will work closely with the PI, postdoctoral researchers, and a multi-institutional team of project partners to integrate ecological data with large-scale environmental and infrastructure datasets. Expected outcomes include peer-reviewed publications, technical reports, and presentations for both scientific and non-scientific audiences. The position offers strong training opportunities in quantitative analysis, interdisciplinary research, and professional development.

Successful candidates will demonstrate strong written and oral communication skills, solid analytical abilities, and the capacity to work independently and collaboratively. Experience or strong interest in fish and aquatic ecology is required. Experience with or interest in computer modeling, statistical analysis (Bayesian and/or frequentist approaches), and GIS is highly desirable.

The selected student will be supported through a combination of Teaching Assistantships (TAships) and Research Assistantships (RAships), for a total of three years of funding.

 Position Description: The Snowden Waterfowl Center of Excellence within the College of forestry, Agriculture, and Natural Resources at the University of Arkansas at Monticello is recruiting applicants for the position of Graduate Research Assistant (GRA) to pursue a Master’s of Science (M.Sc.) degree in Forest Resources studying the spatial arrangement of habitat components including bottomland hardwood reforestation on habitat suitability for midcontinent mallards. Specific aspects of the study will include the construction of a user-friendly, ArcGIS online decision support tool for prioritizing areas for reforestation that will maximize co-benefits for waterfowl. Thus, restoration and reforestation effects are of utmost priority in the region and newly emerging carbon credit markets may provide the catalyst needed to accelerate reforestation in the region to improve habitat suitability for wintering mallards. A graduate assistantship for a master’s student is expected to be funded at Colorado State University (Fort Collins, CO) working with Dr. Brian D. -          Desire to learn or expand on coding and statistical modeling knowledge and skills
-          Desire to collaborate with state wildlife management agencies

M.S. Opportunity: Riparian restoration tools in working grasslands
The Genomics, Ecology, and Modeling for Conservation Lab at North Dakota State University, led by Travis Seaborn, is recruiting for one M.S. position to join our team working on a recently funded project in collaboration with the Albert K. Ekre Grassland Preserve. For more information on the preserve see: https://ndsufoundation.com/magazine/2021/09/ekre-grassland-preserve. 
 Anticipated start date: Summer 2026. Stiped ~$25,000 for 2-3 years. Tuition waiver also provided.
 The overall project will advance our ability to understand community responses to riparian restoration. Riparian ecosystems in the Northern Great Plains have been heavily altered by anthropogenic activities. Although there are numerous restoration options for riparian ecosystems, a common and effective restoration practice, in particular in incised stream systems, are beaver dam analogs. Using streams at the Ekre Grassland Preserve and nearby public land, we will be looking to do a restoration project using invasive buckthorn woody materials. To achieve this, we are beginning to plan a Before-After-Control-Impact design to assess riparian and floodplain ecosystem responses, including geomorphology, biological community, and water quality. Much of the beaver dam analog research that has been done has occurred in the western United States, and response to these activities in the Northern Great Plains is unknown. Surveys of the biological community may include electrofishing and minnow trapping for fish, camera traps for mammals, visual and auditory surveys for birds, and plant identification along transects.
 The primary goals of this position include:
1.    Identify the impact of beaver dam analogs.
2.    Using geographic information systems, develop beaver species distribution models for the region.
 To apply: Please email travis.seaborn@ndsu.edu a letter of interest, which should include an explanation of fit and past relevant experience, and CV by February 20th.

Project Background: 

We are hiring an MS student to examine whether foraging behavior metrics, like grazing bout duration and velocity while grazing, predict diet quality and average daily weight gain of beef cows on central Arizona rangelands. This region contains a wealth of native biodiversity with ecosystems ranging from mixed desert scrub, pinyon-juniper woodlands, and high-elevation ponderosa pine forest. The student will be co-advised by Drs. Funding is available for 2 years and includes salary, tuition, and health insurance. The student will be based in Tucson, AZ but will conduct field work at the University of Arizona V-V Ranch near Rimrock, AZ. Tasks will consist of attaching GPS ear tags to cattle, conducting field behavioral observations, collecting fecal samples, and analysis of movement data. 

The University of Arizona is the state’s land grant university, located in Tucson, Arizona. The University of Arizona is on the land and territories of many Indigenous peoples; today, Arizona is home to 22 federally recognized tribes, with Tucson being home to the O’odham and the Yaqui.

Position Description: We are recruiting one M.S. student/one Ph.D. student to conduct research on “wetland ecology”. Our research team is dedicated to exploring various aspects of wetland ecology. Our main research areas include the eco-hydrological processes of coastal wetlands, biodiversity in Beijing, and the ecology of wetlands in Beijing. We strive to understand the complex relationships between wetland ecosystems and their surrounding environments by field study and modeling, aiming to contribute to the conservation and sustainable management of wetland resources.
By joining our team, students will have the opportunity to work with experienced researchers and use advanced research facilities. They will be immersed in a vibrant academic atmosphere and engage in in-depth studies on wetland ecology, which is of great significance in today's context of environmental protection and ecological restoration.

·        Conduct in-depth research on specific topics within the scope of our team's research areas, such as detailed investigations into the mechanisms of eco-hydrological processes in coastal wetlands or comprehensive analyses of the biodiversity patterns in Beijing's wetlands.

·        Keep up-to-date with the latest research advancements in wetland ecology both domestically and internationally, and contribute to the academic progress of the field through publishing high-quality research papers in renowned academic journals.
·        Participate in academic seminars, workshops, and collaborative projects within the team and with other relevant institutions, actively sharing ideas and insights.

·        Assist in research projects related to wetland ecology, such as helping with field investigations of Beijing's wetland ecosystems or data collection for studies on wetland biodiversity.

·        Participate in regular team discussions and academic activities, presenting their own research progress and ideas, and learning from the experiences of others.

·        Advanced skills in programming languages such as GIS (Geographic Information System), R, and Python. Experience in using these tools for data analysis, spatial analysis, and modeling related to wetland ecology is a plus. For example, being able to use GIS to analyze wetland spatial distribution patterns, R or Python for statistical analysis of ecological data.

Description
I am seeking two motivated master’s students with an interest in crop physiology and environmental stress research. Our research program focuses on understanding how plants perceive and adapt to adverse environmental conditions, with the ultimate goal of protecting crops and mitigating damage caused by environmental stress.

Tomato will be used as the primary research model, as it is both one of the most important vegetable crops worldwide and an excellent model plant for environmental science research. Students will grow tomato plants in our greenhouse, harvest fruits at the mature green stage, and store them under different temperature conditions to investigate the effects of heat stress on fruit ripening.

Project 1: Stable Carbon Isotope Fractionation and Fruit Respiration
One student will focus on developing a novel approach using stable carbon isotope fractionation to monitor the effects of heat stress on fruit respiration pathways, which are closely linked to fruit productivity. Although stable isotope fractionation is widely used in geochemistry, it has rarely been applied to the study of fruit ripening. This approach will provide a multidimensional perspective on how heat stress influences fruit respiratory metabolism. This project includes a collaboration with Rice University, where the student will spend approximately one week each year conducting specialized isotope measurements.

Project 2: Role of Abscisic Acid (ABA) in Heat Stress Tolerance
The second student will investigate the role of the plant hormone abscisic acid (ABA) in tomato plant development and fruit ripening, with a particular focus on its involvement in heat stress responses and resistance mechanisms. This project will compare wild-type tomatoes with mutant lines that have reduced or enhanced ABA accumulation in fruits, with the goal of understanding how ABA influences fruit survival under heat stress conditions.

Through two years of research training, students will gain a strong foundation in the concepts and techniques of environmental stress research, develop proficiency with relevant laboratory and greenhouse instrumentation, and acquire skills essential for careers in environmental science research, agricultural chemistry, and environmental monitoring.

Funding and Qualifications
Prospective students with an interest in agricultural chemistry are encouraged to apply. Students will be supported as teaching assistants, receiving a $15,000 annual stipend and $7,000 in tuition remission, distributed equally across the three academic terms.

Applicants should have a bachelor’s degree in chemistry, biology, agriculture, environmental science, or a related discipline, along with strong written and verbal communication skills and the ability to work both independently and as part of a research team.

Applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis, with the position closing on March 31, 2026. The anticipated start date is September 2026.
